item.title: Wafer.ai runs Kimi K3 model on AMD MI355X GPUs achieving better performance per dollar than Nvidia B300 and B200 nodes [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Wafer.ai reports running the large Kimi K3 open source AI model, with 2.8 trillion parameters, on AMD MI355X GPUs, which have 288GB VRAM and cost significantly less than Nvidia B300 and B200 GPUs. Despite AMD's software challenges, Wafer.ai optimized kernel and model performance to achieve over 3.8 times the throughput per node compared to their Nvidia B200 setup and better cost efficiency than the B300. The MI355X's high memory capacity allows it to serve the large Kimi K3 model on a single node, avoiding the cross-node overhead seen with Nvidia B200 configurations. Wafer.ai addressed initial software issues such as missing kernel functions on ROCm and improved speculative decoding and prefill performance, resulting in substantial throughput gains and competitive latency. This demonstrates AMD GPUs as a cost-effective alternative for serving frontier large language models despite initial software limitations.

item.title: PublicDomainReview explores the Ars Notoria, a medieval manuscript promising rapid mastery of knowledge through magical diagrams and prayers, despite church condemnation
item.description: The Ars Notoria is a medieval text that claimed to accelerate learning through complex diagrams, incantations, and rituals, offering contact with spiritual forces and divine knowledge. Although condemned by theologians like St. Thomas Aquinas as futile and demonic, the manuscript persisted in religious institutions and was copied and printed into the early modern period. The text's unique approach involved symbolic and geometric patterns combined with prayers in ancient languages, aiming to grant scholars instant knowledge without years of study. Its survival and continued interest highlight the tension between medieval scholarly ambition and church doctrine regarding superstition and magic.

item.title: Mozilla publishes inaugural State of Open Source AI report showing open models close performance gap with proprietary AI but capture only 4% of revenue [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Mozilla's first State of Open Source AI report reveals that open AI models have narrowed the performance gap with leading proprietary systems like ChatGPT to 3%, while costs have dropped up to 50 times in three years. Despite powering about a third of real-world AI usage, open models capture only 4% of the revenue, highlighting a disconnect between value and financial return to the open ecosystem. The report, based on a global survey of over 950 developers, finds that Asia leads in open source AI adoption at 89%, with governments in the EU, Canada, and India investing in open AI infrastructure as a strategic asset. While 79% of developers use open models, only 51% have deployed them in production due to missing infrastructure and tooling. Mozilla emphasizes that control over the software layer managing AI behavior is becoming more important than the models themselves, warning that without investment in governance and infrastructure, closed AI systems may dominate, limiting public interest and technological sovereignty.

item.title: YouTube updates AI to reduce low-quality content impact on trusted channels
item.description: YouTube has adjusted its AI algorithms to better protect established, reputable channels from the effects of low-quality or spammy content. This change aims to ensure that known good channels maintain their visibility and audience engagement despite the presence of less reliable uploads on the platform.

item.title: Pluralistic reports executives exaggerate AI's business impact amid coordination pressures to maintain optimism [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Pluralistic explores how corporate leaders often overstate AI's transformative effects on business due to pressures to align with optimistic narratives and avoid job risks. The article draws on insights from Nikhil Suresh of Hermit Tech, who has spoken with hundreds of executives and employees revealing a pattern of AI hype that lacks concrete evidence of significant change. Suresh highlights a coordination problem where executives feel compelled to affirm AI's benefits to preserve their positions, even when actual gains are limited. This dynamic leads to a cycle of mutual reinforcement of AI optimism despite skepticism among subordinates, contributing to what is described as "AI mania" in corporate decision-making.

item.title: XCREENER launches MCP server enabling AI agents to run and validate market screening queries in plain English across multiple asset classes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: XCREENER has released a local stdio MCP server that bridges its XQL screener API, allowing AI agents and developers to validate, explain, and execute market screening queries using plain English commands. The server supports multiple markets including Crypto, Forex, Indices, Commodities, and Metals, and integrates with clients like Claude Desktop, Cursor, and Windsurf without requiring manual HTTP setup. The MCP server exposes tools for query validation, explanation, and execution, enabling users to screen live market data across asset classes simultaneously. Example use cases include identifying oversold instruments, providing market snapshots, and analyzing currency strength, all through natural language inputs translated into XQL queries. Installation options include prebuilt packages and source builds, with API key authentication handled lazily during query execution.

item.title: EU AI Act requires labeling of AI-generated deepfakes and interactive AI systems starting August 2, with compliance deadlines extending to December
item.description: The European Union's AI Act mandates that AI-generated or manipulated content that could be mistaken for real, including deepfakes and interactive AI systems like chatbots, must be clearly labeled starting August 2. This transparency requirement aims to help users identify synthetic media and distinguish it from human-generated content, with a grace period until December 2 for existing generative AI tools to implement machine-readable labels. The rules apply broadly to providers and deployers whose AI outputs are used within the EU, including those outside the region if their content targets EU audiences. Exemptions exist for artistic, satirical, fictional, or editorially reviewed AI-generated text. A Code of Practice developed by independent experts supports compliance, though enforcement and adherence by large platforms and foreign providers remain to be seen.

item.description: The article discusses concerns about the increasing control and influence of artificial intelligence in society. It argues against yielding to AI authority and emphasizes the importance of maintaining human decision-making and independence in the face of advancing AI technologies.

item.title: EU launches voluntary Code of Practice for transparency of AI-generated content starting August 2026 to support compliance with AI Act Article 50 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Starting August 2026, the European Union will implement a voluntary Code of Practice to enhance transparency in AI-generated content, supporting compliance with the AI Act's legal obligations on marking and labeling such content. The code, developed by independent experts and stakeholders, provides practical guidelines for providers and deployers of generative AI systems to mark AI outputs and label deepfakes, aiming to reduce administrative burdens and increase trust across EU member states. The Code of Practice complements the AI Act's transparency requirements under Article 50, addressing risks of deception and manipulation in digital communications. While adherence to the code is voluntary, it offers a recognized framework for demonstrating compliance, with signatories collaborating through task forces to share best practices. By the end of July 2026, around 190 organizations had signed the code, which includes provisions for machine-readable marking and detection of AI-generated content and guidelines for labeling AI-manipulated text and media.

item.title: Pippa launches AI video platform paying artists royalties for style use amid ongoing ethical debates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Pippa, a new AI startup, offers a text-to-video service that compensates artists with royalties whenever their style is used in generated content, aiming to address ethical concerns in generative AI. The company has signed agreements with a few artists and pays them per image and video second generated, alongside a share of subscription revenue, but payments remain modest compared to user fees. Despite its ethical positioning, Pippa's technology still relies partly on models initially trained on internet-scraped art without explicit consent, reflecting a broader challenge in the AI industry. The company hopes to transition fully to artist-provided datasets but faces skepticism from artists wary of community backlash and the legacy of unauthorized training practices. Pippa's founders compare their approach to the music industry's shift from piracy to paid streaming, aiming to set a new standard for AI content generation that respects creators' rights. However, the platform is still early-stage with limited artist participation and must overcome both technical and cultural hurdles to gain wider acceptance among artists and users.

item.title: EU enacts AI Act requiring companies to disclose AI use and comply with risk-based rules starting December 2026 [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: The European Union has introduced the AI Act, the first comprehensive legal framework regulating artificial intelligence, which mandates companies operating in member states to be transparent about their AI applications. The regulation aims to foster trustworthy AI by addressing risks and ensuring safety, fundamental rights, and human-centric AI across various sectors. The AI Act classifies AI systems into risk categories, banning those deemed unacceptable and imposing strict requirements on high-risk AI use cases such as critical infrastructure, education, employment, and law enforcement. The regulation also includes voluntary initiatives like the AI Pact to support early compliance and provides guidelines to help stakeholders understand prohibited practices and the scope of the law. The new rules take effect starting December 2026, positioning Europe as a global leader in AI governance.

item.title: Australian booksellers warn rare books are being destroyed for AI training data amid unusual bulk orders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Australian secondhand booksellers have raised concerns that rare and valuable books are being destroyed to supply data for generative AI training. The practice, revealed in a US lawsuit against AI company Anthropic, involves buying physical books, scanning them after removing spines, and then pulping the remains, which some Australian vendors suspect is happening through intermediaries placing large, atypical orders. Several booksellers reported receiving bulk orders from a Canadian company called Zoom Books, which buys a wide range of titles, including rare and niche items, often without regard to price. While some sellers see the sales as beneficial for clearing stock, they worry about the loss of unique cultural artifacts and the ethical implications of destroying physical books for AI data. The issue highlights tensions between copyright law, AI development, and preservation of literary heritage.

item.description: Librarian.net has released a detailed guide for users seeking to disable or avoid intrusive AI features in their technology environments. The guide covers a range of platforms and applications, including Adobe Acrobat, Android Gemini, Apple Intelligence & Siri, and various web browsers such as Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and DuckDuckGo, providing step-by-step instructions for turning off AI functionalities. The guide addresses common user concerns about unwanted AI integration and offers specific settings adjustments for disabling AI assistants, generative AI options, and AI-enhanced search results. It also includes advice on managing AI features in Google Workspace products like Gmail and Google Docs, aiming to help users maintain control over AI presence in their digital tools.

item.title: OpenAI launches Presence to deploy AI agents for enterprise customer service and internal workflows with engineering support [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI has introduced Presence, a new enterprise product designed to make AI agents production-ready for customer service and internal business workflows. Unlike its existing Workspace Agents, which focus on internal use, Presence targets external deployments and offers direct engineering support for complex cases. Presence is currently available to qualifying enterprise customers but is not broadly open. OpenAI's Forward Deployed Engineers assist clients by selecting workflows, integrating systems, setting guidelines, and managing testing through production launch. The company has not yet clarified how Presence will comply with regulations like the EU AI Act, mentioning trust mechanisms without providing legal specifics.

item.title: Meta AI deploys a second AI agent as a memory coach to reduce errors and improve performance on long tasks by up to 8.3 percentage points [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Meta AI has developed a system where a secondary AI agent acts as a memory coach to help primary AI agents avoid repeating errors and forgetting constraints during complex tasks. This memory agent maintains a structured memory bank and selectively decides when to remind the main agent, improving task success rates across benchmarks. The memory system divides information into private status, knowledge memory, and procedural memory, updating these through predefined tool calls. Tested on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and tau2-Bench, the approach increased task completion rates by up to 8.3 percentage points, with varying improvements across different domains. The selective reminder strategy outperformed constant recall and other memory methods, demonstrating benefits beyond compensating for weaker models.

item.title: Apple caps bug bounty submissions after AI-generated reports clog inbox, delaying disclosure of a $200K macOS vulnerability [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Apple's bug bounty program is overwhelmed by low-quality, AI-generated vulnerability reports, leading the company to limit the number of submissions per researcher. This backlog prevented Italian startup Bynario from reporting a serious macOS flaw that could allow full machine control, which the startup estimates could be worth $100,000 to $200,000 on the black market. Apple has since contacted Bynario regarding the issue. Apple is simultaneously using AI tools from Anthropic and OpenAI to identify vulnerabilities, with recent updates including five times the usual number of fixes. The surge in AI-generated reports raises concerns about the long-term viability of traditional bug bounty programs as companies increasingly rely on automated vulnerability discovery and validation.

DeepSeek-V4-Flash provides advanced coding capabilities but lacks vision, which is supplemented by Luna's multimodal features, while Antigravity CLI handles web search to provide up-to-date information. The integration allows the user to leverage their ChatGPT subscription alongside DeepSeek's API for coding tasks, use Luna for image recognition and vision processing, and employ Antigravity CLI for Google-powered search results. This setup bypasses limitations in standard harnesses by enabling seamless multimodal input and real-time search, enhancing the overall AI agent experience.

item.title: GitHub releases fixed harness and evaluation code for comparing large language model agent memory systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: GitHub hosts the public evaluation code and answer-generation contracts used by the Agent Memory Leaderboard to benchmark large language model (LLM) agent memory systems. The released scripts support Python 3.10+, require external service credentials, and include detailed runtime parameters for tasks such as adding, searching, answering, and judging memory records. The evaluation framework specifies concurrency limits, timeouts, retry policies, and scoring methods, ensuring consistent and reproducible comparisons across datasets. Internal deployment details and sensitive credentials remain undisclosed, focusing the release on transparent evaluation methodology and public dataset compatibility.

item.title: Rails Agent launches fullstack framework for building autonomous AI agents natively in Ruby on Rails with cloud runtime and integrated monitoring [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Rails Agent introduces a fullstack framework that enables developers to build, test, deploy, and monitor autonomous AI agents directly within Ruby on Rails applications. The platform supports Rails 7+ and Ruby 3.2+, providing a Rails-native DSL, integrated documentation, and cloud runtime to simplify AI agent development without requiring AI expertise. The framework includes features such as encrypted provider key management, scalable infrastructure with autoscaling and retries, unified monitoring and debugging, and one-click connectors to over 1,000 apps like Google Sheets and Slack. Agents are organized as directories within Rails apps, allowing developers to write agent logic in plain Ruby classes and manage knowledge, workflows, and memory without external dependencies like vector databases or Redis.

item.title: Why Apple Should Buy Granola [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: • The Big Read: Silicon Valley looks to a new biotech frontier-Montana • Garry Tan's political dreams require this 32-year-old's 'grunt' force • Plus, Recommendations-our weekly pop culture picks: "Dead Rabbit," "The Amateur" and "The Drama" Here's a thought that would've seemed startling not long ago: There's a very good chance that someone secretly recorded you this week with the help of AI. If it didn't happen this week, it will almost certainly happen sometime in the very near future-then continue to happen with greater and greater frequency. And if you weren't the one unknowingly recorded, you might have been the one pushing the record button, and you probably didn't think twice about it. Because here's another thought that once would have seemed extraordinary: Despite what would seem like obvious privacy invasion concerns, no one seems all too bothered by the trend-and the AI note-taking apps fueling it. Of those apps, one of the most popular is Granola, which records a meeting, autogenerates notes from it and suggests follow-up tasks. It can be used for in-person meetings, and it also syncs seamlessly with software like Zoom and Google Meet. And really, I think it's a pretty clear comment on the app's caliber that anyone would rather use Granola than rely on the note-taking features Zoom and Google Meet offer. (People like it for a variety of factors, including the fact that it records digital meetings unobtrusively: No one in a Google Meet would know you're using it-it doesn't join the meeting as a participant or put up a recording banner.) Granola is especially well liked especially in Silicon Valley, where the VC crowd has proselytized it. In a testament to Granola's quality, the company accomplished a real feat a couple of days ago: It released a version of its app for the Apple Watch, and all of a sudden, people were talking online about the Apple Watch as an honest-to-goodness must-have gadget. "We've had a lot of emails saying, 'I'm gonna go out and buy a Watch because of this' or 'Time to pull my Watch out of the drawer,'" said Granola co-founder Sam Stephenson. When was the last time Apple managed to release an attention-grabbing AI feature-or make the Apple Watch seem cool? Certainly not anytime in recent memory. So here's what I think should happen: Apple should buy Granola. Like the best Apple products, Granola is beloved by its fans-many bands would love to have such dedicated groupies-for its sleek, well-designed simplicity. And the startup has just proven it can breathe new life into an Apple product that has seemed dull for years. Apple needs people who can pull off such a task, having chosen to heavily rely on updates to a few core products in recent years. (Granted, maybe incoming CEO John Ternus will shift that mindset a bit; meanwhile, Apple is reportedly working on smart glasses, as well as a wearable AI pin.) Perhaps most importantly, Granola can be probably acquired for the type of price Apple likes to pay: The company does not do mega-acquisitions. Granola, founded in 2023, most recently got a $1.5 billion valuation in a March fundraising, which included Index Ventures, Kleiner Perkins and other investors. Granola's attention-catching Apple Watch debut was something of a happy accident, Stephenson said. The app was originally a side project of Tom Humphrey, a Granola software engineer, that gained momentum within the company after he bolstered enthusiasm for it with a surprising revelation: The data Granola accessed about its iOS users showed that 40% of them also owned an Apple Watch. Among Granola staff, the Apple Watch app has quickly become much more popular than the iPhone one. "You just think to turn it on much more often than you do with the iPhone," Stephenson said. "The worst thing about the iPhone app is that it's in your pocket: out of sight, out of mind. You forget to use it." Granola has toyed with the thought of making its own hardware but has shied away from doing so. Whatever the startup released would face stiff competition from the growing number of already available devices dedicated to AI note-taking. Plaud, a five-year-old startup, makes one of the most popular ones. I first wrote about Granola and AI note-taking last year when it seemed like the dawn of a new always-on, always-recording world. It's now something like sunshiny midmorning: Over the past year, Granola's user growth has been a "smooth curve: upward and to the right," said Stephenson. (He declined to give specifics.) Meanwhile, the startup has gone from two floors of a Shoreditch, London, office to occupying the entire building, roughly quintupling its staff to nearly 100. Given Granola's rising popularity, I asked Stephenson if he had met any unexpected users. "Well, Gwyneth Paltrow comes to mind," he said.-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) Weekend's Latest Stories The Big Read Silicon Valley Looks to a New Biotech Frontier: Montana The state is now allowing anyone-not just the very sick-to access unapproved, experimental drugs. It's a boon for biotech startups and an overt embrace of the tech world ethos for cutting back on rules that might limit innovation. Garry Tan's Political Dreams Require This 32-Year-Old's 'Grunt' Force Forrest Liu is tasked with an agenda that focuses on local Bay Area candidates, economic growth-and the death of the billionaire's tax. Listening: "Dead Rabbit" As a genre of fiction, folk horror has given us memorable entertainment such as "Midsommar" and "The Wicker Man." "Dead Rabbit," a podcast from BBC Radio 4, is the rare nonfiction version: Hosts Dan Ashby and Lucy Taylor, a husband-and-wife pair of investigative journalists, set off into the countryside to figure out why piles of mangled animals keep getting threateningly piled up around Awbridge, England, a well-heeled, 757-person community. It's a place full of well-tended flower baskets and a chipper vicar, who tries to turn the first grisly mise-en-scène he encounters on his parish doorstep-a severed deer's head-into a joke about venison sausages. Not everyone in the clergyman's flock is as determinedly upbeat, and the carcasses have thoroughly disturbed much of the village, sparking WhatsApp groups replete with theories (devil worship, perhaps?) and recriminations. The series begins as a spotlight on what happens within the unnerved small town and then widens its focus to larger issues of conservation, animal cruelty and liberal-versus-conservative politics. Squished roadkill has never seemed more sinister.-Abram Brown Reading: "The Amateur" by Chris Bohjalian After three decades and 24 novels, Chris Bohjalian has established himself as an ultrareliable source of highbrow potboilers. More often than not, he likes to get them going with a real bang. Or, as he described it in a 2018 conversation with The New York Times, he likes an opening moment of "cataclysmic disequilibrium." Just such a catastrophe unfolds in the first few pages of "The Amateur," his latest and probably finest novel. On Aug. 3, 1978, Mira Wilston, a privileged teenage golf prodigy from a tony Westchester, N.Y., suburb, sends a well-struck drive straight through a practice net-and it zings right into the head of a nearby caddie: Kenny, a high school classmate. It kills him instantly. So who deserves the blame? Mira, who narrates the tale? The country club? The net's manufacturer? Had Bohjalian been thinking less ambitiously, he would've kept his exploration of culpability and responsibility confined to the immediate damage from Mira's errant shot (in a tale embellished by nice period-piece details, like the high school's smoking lounge and the Miami Sound Machine records). But he wasn't and he didn't. In the accident's aftermath, the disequilibrium intensifies-as Kenny's demise inadvertently leads to the public revelation of a long-running sexual relationship between Mira, 18, and one of the country club dads. Yes, it should sound a little like "Lolita," and therein lies the greater conceit of "The Amateur," which appropriates and restyles Vladimir Nabokov's classic, widening to an examination of power, control and fate. The connection between the two novels is an explicit one: Mira, who recounts all the events with a meta, tragicomic awareness, remarks on it several times.-A.B. Watching: "The Drama" An admission I make with no degree of hyperbole: I watched several parts of "The Drama," an A24 film starring Robert Pattinson and Zendaya as a pair of engaged lovebirds, with my mouth fully agape. And when the tension between them ratcheted up further, I watched through gaps between my fingers: I'd thrown a hand over my eyes. What can I say? Scenes of matrimonial Armageddon make me squirm, and "The Drama" (newly streaming on HBO Max) goes full-on scorched earth. To explain the plot in much detail would ruin the film, so to summarize it quickly: Shortly before their big day, a secret-telling drinking game goes horribly awry when Emma (Zendaya) reveals a dark moment from her past that shocks Charlie (Pattinson). I don't blame him-it shocked me, too, and what's more surprising is that the film does the reveal quite quickly. (Drew Barrymore survived only marginally longer in "Scream.") Mostly, "The Drama" devotes itself to chronicling the subsequent fallout-with director Kristoffer Borgli twisting the usual rhythms of a screwball rom-com into devious knots. As an unmarried 37-year-old who has needed to soldier through more than a dozen friend weddings in the last decade, I also appreciated how "The Drama" very neatly satirizes how millennials have turned the exchanging of vows into an industrial nuptial complex.-A.B.
